subject: physics_2
question_text: Three resistors each of resistance 10 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the effective resistance of the combination.

verification.note: THE MARK SPLIT NEEDS A TEACHER MORE THAN ANY OTHER CARD IN THIS CHAPTER. This is a SHORT NUMERICAL that the book prints under LONG ANSWER numbering (p31, LAQ 4), with no Problems banner over it, so it is authored as an 8-mark Section C question. But a two-line parallel calculation does not naturally carry eight marks, and the 1+2+2+2+1 split here is INVENTED outright — it is a guess at how an examiner would spread eight marks over a calculation this short, not a scheme anyone has confirmed. A Telangana IPE teacher must rule on both the split AND on whether this question is really examined at 8 marks at all. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE as well: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Transcription: the book prints 'are connected parallel'; the dropped 'in' is restored. Hand-checked: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/10 + 1/10 = 3/10, so R = 10/3 Ω ≈ 3.33 Ω — the same answer the book prints.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The given values
lines: Three resistors are joined in parallel, each
Required: the effective resistance R of the
steps.margin_note: One mark. Write the given values and what is asked before any formula.
steps.why: Setting out the given values and the required quantity first fixes which formula is needed, and it is the line an examiner looks for at the top of a numerical.
common_mistakes: Starting with numbers and no statement of what is given.

recall.must_convey: That the three resistances are each 10 ohm and the effective resistance of the parallel combination is required.
accept: three resistors each ten ohm in parallel
R one R two R three are ten ohm

steps.memory_tip: Given first, required second, formula third.

steps.label: The parallel rule
lines: In a parallel combination the same potential
difference sits across every resistor, so the
Dividing through by the common V,
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The reciprocal rule, with one line saying where it comes from.
steps.why: Every branch is joined across the same two points, so each carries V/R of its own. Adding the currents and dividing by V turns the current sum into a sum of reciprocals.
common_mistakes: Adding the resistances directly. That is the series rule.
Writing R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃, dropping the reciprocal on the left.

recall.must_convey: That in parallel the reciprocals of the resistances add, one by R equals one by R one plus one by R two plus one by R three.
accept: one by R equals sum of one by R one etcetera

steps.memory_tip: Parallel adds currents, so it adds reciprocals of resistance.

steps.label: The substitution
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Show the three separate terms before adding them.
steps.why: Writing the three equal terms out before adding keeps the count visible. With three equal resistances the sum is simply three times one of them.
common_mistakes: Adding only two of the three terms.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives one by ten three times, which adds to three by ten.
accept: one by ten plus one by ten plus one by ten

steps.memory_tip: Three equal terms: keep them separate on the page, then add.

steps.label: The effective resistance
lines: Taking the reciprocal of both sides,
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Invert 3/10 and give the unit. The last step is the one most often skipped.
steps.why: The rule gives 1/R, not R, so the answer is only reached after the reciprocal is taken. Leaving 3/10 as the answer would be a resistance of 0.3 Ω, which is ten times too small.
common_mistakes: Giving 3/10 Ω as the answer. That is 1/R, not R.
Leaving the unit off the final line.

recall.must_convey: That taking the reciprocal gives R equal to ten by three ohm, about 3.33 ohm.
accept: R equals ten by three ohm
reject: one by R equals three by ten

steps.memory_tip: The formula ends at 1/R. Turn it upside down before writing the answer.

steps.label: The check
lines: Check: n equal resistors of resistance x in
parallel give x/n. Here x = 10 Ω and n = 3,
The effective resistance is smaller than any
one of the three resistors, as it must be for
steps.margin_note: One mark. A one-line check that the answer is smaller than the smallest resistor.
steps.why: Adding a parallel branch opens another path for the current, so the combination always conducts better than any single branch. Any parallel answer larger than the smallest resistor is wrong.
common_mistakes: Reporting an answer larger than 10 Ω without noticing it cannot be right.

recall.must_convey: That n equal resistors in parallel give x by n, and that a parallel result must be smaller than the smallest resistor.
accept: x by n for n equal resistors
parallel result is always the smallest
reject: one by ten plus one by ten plus one by ten

steps.memory_tip: A parallel answer is always below the smallest resistor in the group.

insider_note: The book prints this as Long Answer 4, so it is written out at full length. The value 10/3 Ω is exact; leave it as a fraction and give 3.33 Ω beside it.
